ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Clinical Psychology Consultation — Frederick Douglass — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Two-week review of the hand and sleep, with clinical psychology evaluation the same day

text.paragraph: A 34-year-old editor, author, and public speaker who survived violence, hunger and cold, and early separation from his mother in childhood and youth, and assaults in adulthood, now has nightmares once or twice a month, watchfulness when traveling, and short sleep. Please evaluate whether he meets criteria for PTSD and advise on treatment and on his sleep, in a trauma-informed way and only with his consent. [S]
Urgency: Routine, within two weeks, on the same day as his two-week primary care visit. [S]

list.item: Does he meet DSM-5-TR criteria for PTSD, or are his symptoms below the threshold?
If PTSD is present, which trauma-focused psychotherapy would you recommend, and would medication help?
What would help his short sleep and the nightmares?
How should primary care monitor him, and when should he come back to you?

text.paragraph: Mr. Douglass is seen at the request of Dr. Pettaway. Before we began I explained what the interview would cover, that he did not need to describe any event in detail, and that he could pause or stop at any time; he agreed. He describes the violence and deprivation of his childhood and youth and the assaults of his adult life plainly and in his own words. Over the past month he has had nightmares about his youth once or twice, and unwanted memories when something reminds him, which pass within minutes. He is watchful when he travels to speak, plans his routes and companions, and is otherwise at ease at home. He does not avoid reminders: he chooses to write and speak about his past, and says the work gives that past a purpose. He does not see himself as damaged or to blame; he is angry at injustice and directs that anger into his work. He sleeps about five hours on working nights because he writes past midnight and wakes early, and lies awake after a nightmare. Concentration and mood are good. He does not drink or use drugs and has no thoughts of suicide. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Frederick Augustus Washington Bailey, later Frederick Douglass, was born into slavery in Talbot County, Maryland, in February 1818; the exact day is not known. He later chose February 14 as his birthday, because that was the last time he saw his mother. [D]

He was separated from his mother as an infant and saw her, to know her as such, no more than four or five times, each time briefly and at night. She died when he was about seven; he was not allowed to be present during her illness, death, or burial. He later wrote that it was "a life-long, standing grief" to him that he knew so little of her. [D]
As a young child on the plantation where he lived from 1824 to 1826 he "suffered much from hunger, but much more from cold," with no shoes or jacket, and his feet were cracked by the frost. [D]
As a small child he witnessed the whipping of his aunt, and wrote, "I never shall forget it whilst I remember any thing." [D]

At about sixteen he was hired out for a year to Edward Covey, a farmer known as a "slave breaker." During the first six months "scarce a week passed without his whipping me"; he wrote that Covey "succeeded in breaking me. I was broken in body, soul, and spirit." The Narrative dates this year to 1833; the National Park Service chronology dates it to 1834. [D]

On a hot August day that year, while carrying wheat to the fan, he broke down with "a violent aching of the head, attended with extreme dizziness" and trembling, and fell; Covey kicked him and struck him on the head. [D]
He then resisted Covey in a fight, and afterwards wrote, "From this time I was never again what might be called fairly whipped, though I remained a slave four years afterwards." [D]

While learning to caulk at a Baltimore shipyard he was attacked by four white apprentices; one kicked him in the left eye with a heavy boot, and he wrote that his "left eye was nearly knocked out" and that the eye was closed and badly swollen. [D]

On September 3, 1838, he escaped to New York; he married Anna Murray, a free Black woman, and they settled in New Bedford, Massachusetts, where he worked as a caulker and took the name Frederick Douglass. [D]
In 1841 he was hired as a lecturer by the Massachusetts Anti-Slavery Society, and in May 1845 he published the Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave. [D]

On September 16, 1843, a pro-slavery mob at Pendleton, Indiana, beat him unconscious and broke his right hand; he continued the lecture tour. He later wrote that "as the bones broken were not properly set, my hand has never recovered its natural strength and dexterity." [D]
From 1845 to 1847 he lectured in Ireland, Scotland, and England; in 1846 British admirers raised the money to buy his freedom, and he returned to the United States legally free in 1847. [D]

In December 1847 he began publishing his own weekly newspaper, The North Star, in Rochester, New York, renamed Frederick Douglass' Paper in 1851; from Rochester he helped hundreds of people escaping slavery as a station master of the Underground Railroad. [D]
On May 5, 1849, he was attacked by a gang while walking along the Battery in New York City with two friends. [D]
As a boy in Baltimore he was taught his letters and then taught himself to write; in 1831 he underwent a religious conversion and joined Bethel A.M.E. Church. [D]
He and Anna Murray Douglass had five children, born between 1839 and 1849. [D]

The project roster lists post-traumatic stress disorder and complex trauma as his anchor conditions. No source fetched for this record diagnoses him, and the label is not adopted as a historical diagnosis. [R]

list.item: Personal history of psychological trauma, with symptoms below the threshold for PTSD (Z91.49). On the CAPS-5 he has intrusion symptoms (occasional nightmares and brief unwanted memories) and two arousal symptoms (watchfulness and sleep disturbance), but no avoidance and no lasting negative change in thinking or mood. PTSD requires at least one avoidance symptom and two negative-cognition or mood symptoms, so the criteria are not met and I am not making a PTSD diagnosis. His watchfulness when traveling is proportionate to real threats he has faced; his anger at injustice is moral conviction, not a symptom. The PCL-5 of 24 agrees. The screening yes to blaming others reflected blame placed where it belongs. [S]

Treatment for PTSD. Not indicated now. If his symptoms rise to the level of PTSD and he wants treatment, the recommended first-line options are individual trauma-focused psychotherapy, cognitive processing therapy or prolonged exposure, delivered weekly. If he prefers medication or psychotherapy is not available, sertraline, paroxetine, or venlafaxine are the recommended medicines. Prazosin is suggested only for nightmares as part of PTSD. [S]

Insufficient sleep with occasional nightmares (Z72.820). The main problem is a short sleep window from late writing and early waking, not insomnia disorder; the nightmares add a few broken nights a month. A brief behavioral approach should help. [S]

Strengths. Purposeful work, his writing, his family and community, and his faith; he taught himself to write as a boy and regards it as the way he made his own life. These are the foundation of the plan. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Dr. Pettaway's intake note, the PC-PTSD-5 and PCL-5 at intake, the PHQ-9 and AUDIT-C, and a structured interview today (CAPS-5). [S]

list.item: No PTSD diagnosis: record his trauma history and the screening results, without a disorder code. [S]

No trauma-focused psychotherapy or medication now; he agrees. Cognitive processing therapy or prolonged exposure, or sertraline, paroxetine, or venlafaxine if he prefers medication, would be the options if PTSD develops and he wants treatment. [S]

Two brief behavioral sleep sessions with me, the first today and the second in two weeks: a fixed waking time, a seven-hour sleep window, no writing in the last hour before bed, and a short routine for nights after a nightmare, with a two-week sleep diary. [S]
PCL-5 and PHQ-9 at each primary care chronic-care visit; return to me if the PCL-5 reaches 31 or more, if function declines, or whenever he wants. [S]
Keep every step consent-based: explain first, ask, and let him choose what to share. [S]
Discussed with Dr. Pettaway the same day. Mr. Douglass heard the findings and the plan, asked how the criteria were applied, and agreed with the plan. [S]
Follow-up: Second sleep session in two weeks. No further routine visits; he may return at any time, and primary care will send him back if his scores rise. [S]
